This guidance was developed in collaboration with the International Civil Aviation Organization, the International Air Transport Association, and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, USA. It provides technical recommendations for Ebola virus disease (EVD) preparedness planning, particularly for entry screening at airports, ports, and land crossings. In August 2014, the WHO Director-General declared the EVD outbreak in West Africa a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005. The IHR Emergency Committee advised unaffected countries to enhance surveillance for clusters of unexplained fever or deaths due to febrile illness. Countries were also advised to prepare to detect, investigate, and manage EVD cases to minimize the risk of international spread while avoiding general bans on international travel and trade. WHO does not recommend entry screening for EVD at this time but suggests that countries may develop entry screening plans based on their risk assessments and cost-benefit analyses. Such procedures should not interfere with international travel and trade. The incubation period for EVD ranges from 2 to 21 days. Individuals without symptoms cannot spread the disease. Transmission primarily occurs through direct contact with the body fluids of symptomatic individuals. Entry screening should be part of a comprehensive approach to disease prevention, treatment, and care. Resources, capacity, and the volume of travelers from affected areas should be considered. Travelers in transit may be prioritized for screening. Airlines should consider educating passengers about EVD and the procedures they may undergo upon arrival. Infection occurs through contact with the blood, body fluids, or tissues of an infected symptomatic person or the body of someone who has died from Ebola. Avoid handling items that may have been contaminated. Symptoms include fever, weakness, muscle pain, headache, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, and, in some cases, bleeding. There is no approved vaccine for EVD. Travelers should practice careful hygiene, especially hand hygiene, and seek immediate medical attention if they feel ill after staying in areas with recent EVD cases. Entry screening involves primary and secondary stages. Primary screening includes temperature checks and visual observation for signs of illness, while secondary screening involves more detailed assessments by medically trained staff. Screening personnel should use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) and follow established protocols. Screening staff should be trained in proper PPE use and procedures for assessing travelers. Secondary screening includes detailed interviews, temperature checks, and assessments for EVD symptoms. Travelers meeting risk criteria may be referred for medical evaluation or public health observation. Data management is critical for recording and analyzing information collected during entry screening. This data helps evaluate the effectiveness of screening programs and informs future decision-making. Legal mechanisms should be in place to support screening activities, including medical evaluations, public health interventions, and travel restrictions for exposed individuals. Coordination with national and local authorities is essential. Entry screening plans should align with public health emergency plans and include provisions for isolating and treating affected travelers, disinfecting contaminated items, and ensuring the safety of screening personnel. Communication strategies should educate travelers and the travel industry about the screening process and its implications. In summary, entry screening is a public health intervention designed to identify individuals at risk of EVD and prevent further travel.
